utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, this afternoon we'll have an illustration of the classical rule of lawyers, that is to assist the Bench, and I do hope the submissions that we will hear will provide a solution to the very difficult problem that we face in getting this trial started. I'm going to give each party 50 minutes and I just remind you of the issues that I'd raised, the question of severance under Rule 82, the question of keeping the trial in the pre-trial phase prompted by Dr. de Man's conclusion that the accused would not be well enough to attend court for another three to six months. The third was also prompted by Dr. de Man's finding of unfitness, perhaps another round of examinations on the question of the accused's fitness, video conference link, number four, what would be the optimum conditions to secure the most efficient and fairest manner for that procedure. The fifth one was starting the trial on Monday the 7th on the basis that the accused would be out of the hospital on the Thursday or Friday of this week and the circumstances that under which we would commence the trial, and then this morning I asked my officers to relay to you another question that I formulated and which I think gets to the root of the issues that we face. In what circumstances, if any, may an accused, one, whose illness prevents him from being present in court; two, who has not waived his right to be present; three, who is represented by counsel; and four, in relation to whom a motion for his unfitness has been rejected, be tried by a Trial Chamber in his absence. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It is my hope that we are of assistance to the Chamber in deciding this difficult question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say that I would prefer if you were to deal with them in the order in which I set them but I appreciate that the issues overlap. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours, apologies for my interruption. We just would seek an oral application that when it concerns detailed citations from the report of Dr. de Man, those could be conducted in private session because we believe that the privacy of the accused should not unnecessarily be invaded. Although Your Honour has ruled that it's now a matter of public interest, we do believe that the report itself contains also information about the private circumstances of the accused which have not yet been disclosed to the public audience. So we respectfully ask the court if the Prosecution intends to cite from that report, and intends to disclose portions of information which have not yet been disclosed, that those portions will be dealt with in private session. We as Defence, we will restrict ourselves by quoting and citing in detail from the report in public session and we hope that the Prosecution and Your Honours could agree that this is something which goes to the direct privacy of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, I understand the submission that you made and perhaps also your duty to make it as counsel for the accused Stanisic, but my decision remains the same. Where the health of an accused has interrupted and interfered with the course of a trial, as the health of this accused has, it becomes a matter of public interest in the Trial Chamber's view, and the proper administration of justice requires that the proceedings, even if they relate to those health conditions be conducted in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would like to preface my submissions on the five questions posed by the Chamber yesterday with a few comments and observations. Yesterday, the Chamber expressed its concern that Mr. Stanisic's health had now become a persistent impediment to the commencement of this trial. The question the Chamber faces and has asked for submissions today is similar to a question posed and answered by the Appeals Chamber in another case which I will discuss later in detail. I'd like to give the Court a short quote from that decision: "How should the Tribunal treat a defendant whose health, while good enough to engage in the ordinary and non-strenuous activities of every day life, is not sufficiently robust to withstand all the rigours of trial work. Must the Trial Chamber be forced to choose between setting that defendant free and allowing the case to grind to an effective halt? In the Appeals Chamber's view, to ask that question is to answer it." That is a quote from the Slobodan Milosevic case, the decision on the interlocutory appeal of the Trial Chamber's decision on the assignment of Defence counsel at paragraph 14. Dr. de Man's report, which has precipitated this discussion today, was an unexpected development given the recent hearings held in this case. Before I address the specific questions posed by the Chamber, it is important at the outset to recognise several important facts. First and foremost, less than a month ago on the 10th of March, this Chamber issued its decision on the motion regarding the fitness to stand trial. This decision is a carefully reasoned decision based upon a comprehensive hearing which fully and carefully explored all of the issues related to Mr. Stanisic's health. It is a decision based upon contemporaneous and reliable evidence that was before the Chamber. It is my view that the findings of the Chamber and the decision that flowed logically and legally from those findings can only be impugned or reconsidered upon a showing with similar, similarly reliable evidence that there has been a change of circumstances over the last couple of weeks. Obviously the focus then turns to whether the report of Dr. de Man does this and I will address this question later in my submissions. Second, during the course of that hearing, the Chamber heard evidence from all of the experts that Mr. Stanisic exhibited no symptoms indicating the presence of a psychosis. While the symptoms significance of psychotic symptoms in a determination of fitness was discussed in the hearing and referenced in the Chamber's decision, it was clear that there was nothing approaching psychotic symptoms last month. The first observation of these was by Dr. de Man last week. The Chamber must carefully scrutinize the findings related to the psychotic features observed by Dr. de Man and consider whether Mr. Stanisic, a man of admittedly high intelligence, could and is now mimicking features he now fully appreciates support his desire to have this case dismissed on the grounds of fitness. Thirdly, there is no basis for any finding that Mr. Stanisic's condition is a permanent or terminal one. Even those experts who suggest that he may be unfit all agree that this condition is treatable and in time he will be in a condition to effectively participate in his trial. The most dire prediction we have regarding how long this will take is from Dr. de Man who says it may take from between 3 and 6 months. Mr. Stanisic has been found fit, he has been found fit by this Trial Chamber, and any colourable claim that he is unfit is a claim of a temporary condition. The first question that the Chamber asked us to address was the issue of a severance. It is the Prosecution's position that any consideration of a severance of Mr. Stanisic is premature at this juncture. While we must be vigilant of how delays occasioned by Mr. Stanisic's health impact the rights of Mr. Simatovic, we have yet to be confronted with a delay that places his rights in jeopardy. The standard is not that his trial commence as soon as possible. He entered this present period of detention less than two months ago and even if the Chamber were to adopt the conclusions of Dr. de Man creating the greatest delay, Mr. Simatovic would be in pre-trial detention for approximately 8 months, a time period clearly falling within an appropriate period. Similarly, it is difficult to conceive of a colourable claim that a delay of six months would result in the loss of evidence or of witnesses Mr. Simatovic might wish to call in his defence. On the 3rd of September, 2000, in the Trial Chamber hearing the Blagoje Simic case, presided over by you, Judge Robinson, the Chamber issued a decision entitled, "Decision on a motion for separate trial for Simo Zaric." That decision resolved a motion by Mr. Zaric seeking a severance under Rule 82(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On page 2 of that decision, the Chamber summarized the basis upon which Mr. Zaric sought severance. Among those reasons are some reasons that are relevant to the Chamber's consideration today. One of the reasons was that the joinder with other accused would result in a delay to the start of the trial for reasons unrelated to Mr. Zaric. The Chamber in denying the motion stated: "That a joint trial avoids duplication of evidence, minimizes hardship to witnesses and is generally in the interests of judicial economy." In short, while we must always have the impact of Mr. Stanisic's illness on Mr. Simatovic in mind, the Prosecution believes that the situation with respect to Mr. Simatovic can be resolved in a manner and in a time-period that will not cause undue prejudice to Mr. Simatovic. The second question, whether or not to adjourn the case for three to six months and leave it in the pre-trial phase. It is the Prosecution's position that it is certainly premature to consider adjourning the case for such a long period. I believe that the Chamber's decision was predicated or the Chamber's question was predicated on Dr. de Man's conclusions that a regime of tricyclic antidepressants Mr. Stanisic could regain fitness in a period of three to six months. My cursory review of the literature and our communication with Dr. Mimica last evening suggests that positive results of tricyclic therapies are most often seen much earlier and in most cases reach full effectiveness in a period of four to six weeks. There is a reference in Dr. Dominecus's report to a change of medicines in February. Although we do not know when Mr. Stanisic was first placed on tricyclics, he may already be on them for several weeks and it is possible that he will realise tangible benefits very shortly. I think the question of what would be an appropriate adjournment is best reserved to my discussion of how we determine Mr. Stanisic's present psychological condition. I think in the resolution of that matter, what if any adjournment is required will become clear. The third question, whether the court should order another round of psychiatric evaluations and a new hearing into the fitness of Mr. Stanisic. As I stated at the beginning of my remarks, the Chamber has less than one month ago issued a carefully reasoned decision based upon its findings after a thorough hearing into the fitness of Mr. Stanisic. It is my position that those findings should stand until such time as it is demonstrated that the circumstances have sufficiently changed to warrant the Chamber to reexamine this issue. The question is whether the report of Dr. de Man does this. For two reasons, the Prosecution does not attach great weight to the report of Dr. de Man, and questions whether it establishes a basis for questioning the Chamber's carefully rendered decision. First, Dr. de Man has been admirably candid about the limitations of his own examination. One, he had a single encounter with Mr. Stanisic. Two, the encounter lasted 60 minutes and the effective time spent with Mr. Stanisic is in reality much less given that the interview was conducted with the assistance of an interpreter. Three, Dr. de Man had absolutely no access to the medical file. Although he notes that Mr. Stanisic gave full permission for access to his medical records, it seems that this came during the evaluation itself and that Dr. de Man was not able to follow up on this. There is nothing in Dr. de Man's report that would indicate that the contents of those reports played a role in his evaluation, and there is some evidence that they did not. For example, Dr. de Man's misstatement of Mr. Stanisic's place of birth, a fact that is indicated correctly on most of the prior medical records. Four, at the time of the evaluation, Mr. Stanisic was being treated for renal colic which is technically the severe pain associated with kidney stones. We have already heard in great detail the relationship that Mr. Stanisic's physical condition has with his mental condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you mentioned that the doctor only had one session with Mr. Stanisic. Is that not the same for the -- most of the doctors who examined him in relation to the hearing that we had? I don't recall that they had more than one session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have at the tip of my fingers the amount of time spent by the other experts but I do note in Dr. de Man's report he suggests that the time that he wanted to spend was limited by the physical condition of Mr. Stanisic, indicating that he did not have an opportunity to conduct a full examination or the examination he would have wanted to have conducted with Mr. Stanisic. And I will try to retrieve the specific information regarding other examinations. Finally, although the exact time and dosage are not indicated, Dr. de Man notes that Mr. Stanisic had taken morphine within 24 hours of the evaluation, so it is quite possible that he was still under the effects of a very powerful analgesic morphine during the time of his examination. The second reason. Despite all of this, Mr. Stanisic's evaluation by Dr. de Man is by and large consistent with the reports that were reviewed by the Trial Chamber during the fitness hearing and which did not constitute, in the Trial Chamber's view, an unfitness to stand trial. The expert consensus is that Mr. Stanisic is depressed, and that this depression is caused by a combination of his present life circumstances, for example, his failed marriage, his incarceration in a foreign country, facing a serious criminal trial, and having -- and being worn down by his intestinal disease and its complications. Those complications include kidney stones, which have a relationship as we know with Mr. Stanisic's pouchitis, and Dr. de Man's opinion fits comfortably within the broad consensus of the other forensic experts that testified before the Chamber. This was not found by the Trial Chamber to constitute unfitness to stand trial. Dr. de Man's evaluation should also not be found to constitute unfitness to stand trial, notwithstanding his use of conclusory language to the effect at the end of his report. As noted above, Mr. Stanisic's depression is a reactive one, and one of the things he is reacting to, by getting depressed, is his physical condition. In that regard, it is significant that Dr. de Man noted a more severe depression than other experts. In particular, he is the first of the seven mental health professionals who has examined Mr. Stanisic to find psychotic features attached to his depressive state. All of the prior psychiatrists and psychologists have affirmatively ruled out psychosis, except for one passing note in a letter by Dr. Blagojevic. With respect to the reference in his report to psychotic features and the visitations or the possible hallucinations he is recently perceiving at night encouraging him to kill himself, it is really not all that different from Dr. Blagojevic's testimony and one wonders could the difference or a different characterisation of those reported symptoms be due to the fact that this particular evaluation was conducted through a translation? Could it be a translation error? Could it be a possible cultural misperception? And yet even in the severe depression, Dr. de Man describes Mr. Stanisic on page 4 of his report as, "Clearly ill and physically suffering but nonetheless alert and cooperative, 57-year-old male who is well-oriented in place, time, and person. The attention span is limited but there are no signs of diminished function of memory, neither are there any signs of cognitive deterioration." Dr. de Man then goes on to describe Mr. Stanisic as having a clear wish to die. This of course must be taken seriously but again the detention unit is probably one of the safest places for a suicidal person given the 24-hour attention that can be paid. While it is up to the Chamber to decide, the Prosecution believes the Chamber could consider Dr. de Man's report and make a determination that in light of its inherent limitations, it does not establish cause to reconsider its recent findings in March based upon what the Prosecution believes is more reliable evidence. It appears that Dr. de Man like some of the other experts drew the conclusion based upon their determination of certain symptomology of unfitness and in some ways usurping the Court's -- the Court making its legal decision of whether those symptoms did constitute true unfitness in the legal sense. The Court, consistent with its responsibility, can consider his observations and yet draw different conclusions than Dr. de Man. In the alternative, the Chamber could convene a relatively limited hearing in which Dr. de Man would appear before this Chamber and discuss his findings related to Mr. Stanisic. It may be that after that hearing, the Chamber finds that his report does not give rise to a reconsideration of its 10th of March decision finding Mr. Stanisic fit. In the event that the Chamber finds that it does reawaken this issue, the Prosecution suggests that the Chamber, having heard from a number of experts, is in a position to direct which experts it wishes to conduct follow-up examinations of Mr. Stanisic. The Chamber may take the view that it will be assisted in making a determination of Mr. Stanisic's present psychological state by follow-up examinations of one or more of the experts that have already testified. As I said yesterday, the Prosecution would seek, if necessary, to have Dr. Mimica conduct a follow-up examination of Mr. Stanisic. We have been in contact with Dr. Mimica and he is willing to conduct such an examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The hearing that you contemplate is -- would be confined to Dr. de Man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I suggest that that would be the first course of action, Your Honour, and if after that, the Court felt that it needed more information, perhaps by psychiatrists and psychologists that have seen Mr. Stanisic on a prior occasion and can perhaps give the Chamber some indication of whether or not there has been a deterioration that the Chamber could then, rather than reconvening or starting from scratch as it were on a fitness hearing, could simply ask some of the experts that testified at the fitness hearing to do a follow-up examination and then report that to the Chamber. Dr. Mimica has also suggested that he would be able to give the Chamber a more complete picture of Mr. Stanisic's mental health if he could include in his report some psychometric tests which would be administered by a psychologist. He is prepared to recommend such a psychologist with whom he has worked and in whose work he has great confidence. In short, the Prosecution recognises that given Dr. de Man's report, the Chamber must satisfy itself that there has been no change of circumstance, but such can be done after a reading of the report or after a hearing strictly limited to this particular issue without having to conduct, once again, a lengthy hearing so shortly after the Court's comprehensive hearing last month. The fourth issue we were asked to address, the feasibility of video conferencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you go on to that, can I ask you: How would the Chamber treat with Dr. de Man's summary that the situation has deteriorated into a clinically significant depression with psychotic features? Is the Chamber to ignore that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I think given the fact that what we know about the relationship between the psychosomatic illness and the psychiatric illness that Mr. Stanisic suffers from, recognising that he was directly in the middle of what perhaps is one of the most painful illnesses or conditions someone can endure, the passing of a kidney stone, and from my conversations with Mr. Knoops yesterday, he indicated that on Friday, the day of this examination, Mr. Stanisic was still very much in extreme pain, so the Court could reach the view that given those circumstances of this evaluation, the pain, the morphine, the limitations placed on Dr. de Man, the Court could reach the view that this report is simply unreliable and rely on the comprehensive reports and evidence that the Chamber heard only a short time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to video conferencing, this morning I had a phone conversation with David Falces who would be the person responsible for administering and supervising the exploration of the ability of current technology to set up video conferencing about -- a video conference link between the courtroom here and the detention unit. Mr. Falces informs me that it would be possible to do the following: One, to establish a secure video link between the court and place in the detention unit from which Mr. Stanisic could effectively participate in the proceedings. The Tribunal already has a leased cable between this building and the detention unit capable of transmitting the proceedings back and forth in a secure manner. 20 of the 60 detainees already have computers in their detention rooms. It would not be complicated matter to provide one to Mr. Stanisic. Two, Mr. Falces also informs me that it is also possible to provide Mr. Stanisic with a secure means of communication with his Defence team by both e-mail during court proceedings and by video conferencing during breaks. A means of communication that would be secure not only from interference from outside the Tribunal but also secure and unreadable to anyone in the Tribunal except the Defence team thereby ensuring that these privileged communications are never inadvertently compromised. I want to convey Mr. Falces's view that although he sees no technological impediment to establishing such links, he is unable to say, without looking into the matter further, how long it would take to set this up. It was my impression that he was talking in terms of weeks and not months in considering the different tasks that would have to be undertaken to establish this system. He advised me that they, in connection with an earlier case, had already made some preliminary exploration of the potential to establish such communication. The next issue which is raised by the Court in asking us to deal with this issue is the legal question. Under what circumstances is participation via videolink legally permissible. And I'd like to examine with the Chamber some of the relevant jurisprudence. The first and perhaps clearest example of when such an arrangement would be permissible is in the case in which the accused expressly waives his right to be physically present for the proceedings. The Milan Simic case is the only ICTY case in which an accused has participated in the trial phase of proceedings via videolink. Milan Simic followed his trial from the detention unit through a videolink due to health reasons, health complications that he was experiencing but he did waive his right to be present in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Am I given to understand that he had pleaded guilty, if I'm not mistaken, so that that puts a different complexion on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will check my information. There are some such as Mrs. Plavcic who pled guilty via videolink but I believe Mr. Simic was someone who had a bad back problem and actually did go through the trial, at least a part of the trial until he pled guilty through a videolink, but I can check that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can check it out, but I understand that it was the sentencing judgement that he followed by video conference link.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will check that further, Your Honour, and perhaps if I could have a few minutes later to clarify that. Currently, in a current case, the Prlic case, the accused Pusic in that case has been absent from court on multiple occasions due to health reasons but there has always been a waiver and there has been no other alternative arrangement for his participation in the trial such as video conferencing. The other scenario would be where there is no waiver and the jurisprudence such as in Barayagwiza there it is permissible where the accused is found to have obstructed the proceedings or has engaged in some conduct which amounts to a waiver. In the Barayagwiza case in the decision of the 2nd of November, 2000, the Chamber found that the trial can continue in the absence of the accused if he is aware of the ongoing trial and voluntarily decides not to attend. Mr. Barayagwiza never attended personally but was represented by counsel. That's indicated in the judgement of the 3rd of December, 2003, at paragraph 83. In paragraph 6 of the November 2000 decision, it reads: "In such circumstances, where the accused has been duly informed of his ongoing trial, neither the Statute nor human rights law prevent the case against him from proceeding in his absence." We can find similar jurisprudence in the cases of the Special Court for Sierra Leone, for example, the Gbao case in a decision decided on the 12th of June, 2004. In another case from the Special Court for Sierra Leone, the Sesay case, a case in which Mr. Jordash will be familiar as he represented the accused, in its decision of the 19th of January, 2005, the Trial Chamber found that the unexplained absence of Mr. Sesay and Mr. Kallon, who were mentally fit and had no known medical condition at the time, perceived their voluntary refusal to attend court as a waiver of their right to attend trial. Also in Article 63 of the ICC Statute, in that case, they adopted the same principle that the use of video technology in certain cases, particularly in where the accused has voluntarily waived their right or has obstructed the process in such a way as to constitute a waiver of the right, that this technology is not deemed to infringe on the basic right of an accused to be present during the trial. Now, the third category, perhaps the one that may be relevant here is where the alternative means might be employed in the case of an accused who through no fault of his own is made to participate via videolink and this was the case in the Zigiranyirazo case in the ICTR. In the ICTR Appeals Chamber decision of the 30th of October 2006, the Appeals Chamber found that when important witnesses testifies, it is not enough for the accused to participate through videolink. It is not equal to being physically present at trial. The Appeals Chamber, its decision on interlocutory appeal in the case of Prosecutor versus Zigiranyirazo is directly relevant to the question of an accused's presence in trial via videolink. In that decision, the Appeals Chamber held that: "An accused's right to be tried in his or her presence implies a right to be physically present at trial." The Chamber concluded this based on: One, a plain reading of Article 20(4)(d) of the ICTR Statute, which is analogous to our Article 21(4)(d). The legal framework of the ICTR and ICTY noting that no rules provide for the participation of an accused in the trial phase via videolink and that Rule 65 bis(C)(ii) gives rise to an inference that participation via video or teleconference is not the same as physical presence. And three, the practice of the ICTY and ICTR noting that the accused have only participated via videolink with their consent. And four, the fact that other international, regional, and national systems share a similar view that the right to be present implies the right to be physically present. The Appeals Chamber did go on to note that the right to physical presence is not an absolute right, but that it was a very important right, and restriction of it must be "in the service of a sufficiently important objective." The Appeals Chamber gave little guidance regarding what might constitute a sufficiently important objective, but they implied that two particularly important considerations were: One, the ability to assess the credibility of witnesses, which the Appeals Chamber seem to hold by inference could not be done by videolink. And two, whether the situation requiring the accused to participate via videolink was the fault of the accused, as where, for example, an accused would disrupt proceedings. The Appeals Chamber also noted that the need to ensure a reasonably expeditious trial was of "general importance." While the jurisprudence might at first glance suggest that participation via videolink is not a suitable substitute for physical presence, this issue merits closer examination. Could there ever be a voluntary waiver? Assuming that Mr. Stanisic never signs a waiver to participate in these proceedings by videolink and we don't know that that's true, but assuming that he doesn't, unless the Trial Chamber finds that the accused is voluntarily absent from the court, by a conduct that is implicit in his actions, it is difficult to continue a trial via videolink to the detention unit. Should Mr. Stanisic fall ill during this trial, even if that illness did not prevent him from viewing the proceedings on video and communicating with his counsel, the present state of the jurisprudence would not clearly support a decision of the Chamber to proceed by way of video conference absent the express consent of Mr. Stanisic to do so and in fact would in simplest terms require an adjournment of proceedings until he can be physically present. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that how you read that case? I had gathered when I read it that it turned on its own facts in that the Appeals Chamber found that the use of video conference link was not the most restrictive -- was not the least restrictive means that could be employed, and it was open to the Trial Chamber to employ some other -- some other device. I didn't read it as outlawing the use of video conference link without the consent of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as Your Honour will hear as my remarks continue, nor does the Prosecution believe it is an absolute bar. What it does talk about is a sufficiently important objective. I believe that there is other jurisprudence which would indicate that the situation that we face here may present a situation where the Court may very well find that videolink conferencing does serve a sufficiently important objective and would allow the Court in a limited way to restrict the right of physical presence in the trial even if Mr. Stanisic should not waive his physical presence in the trial. But going back to another possibility for how the Chamber might employ video conferencing. If on a particular day, the Chamber finds that Mr. Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies. If on a particular day, the Chamber finds that Mr. Stanisic, despite his chronic medical complaints, is physically and mentally fit to come to court and then declines to do so, the Chamber would be entitled to find that such a voluntary refusal with no medical basis constitutes a voluntary waiver and would be entitled to proceed via videolink. As Zigiranyirazo states, the right of an accused to be physically present at trial is not absolute but that the right is fundamental right that can only be restricted "in service of a sufficiently important objective." In addition to any restriction, "must impair the right no more than is necessary to accomplish the objective." A decision in another case sheds light on what constitutes a sufficiently important objective, to justify the restriction of a similar fundamental right. In the decision on interlocutory appeal of the Trial Chamber's decision on the assignment of defence counsel in the Slobodan Milosevic case, the Appeals Chamber states that the right to representation is an "indispensable cornerstone of justice" on a "structural par" with rights such as the right to remain silent, the right to confront witnesses, and the right to a speedy trial. More significantly for our case, the Appeals Chamber specifically drew a parallel between the right to self-representation, and the right of an accused to be tried in his presence, saying that the comparison of the two rights is particularly instructive and emphasizing that the accused's right to be present at trial and the right to self-representation are "listed in the same string of rights and indeed the same clause" of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber clearly views the two rights as being of similar importance. Despite the fundamental nature of the right to self-representation, the Appeals Chamber nevertheless acknowledged that the right to self-representation could be curtailed on the grounds that a defendant's self-representation is substantially and persistently obstructing the proper and expeditious conduct of his trial. It is particularly significant that the Appeals Chamber made this holding in a context in which it was the health of the accused that caused his right to self-representation to disrupt the trial, rather than any intentional, blameworthy, disruptive behaviour on the part of the accused. Indeed, the Appeals Chamber goes on to say that intentional disruption of the trial by an accused is not the only kind of disruption of the trial that justifies the restriction of the fundamental right to self-representation. Specifically, the Chamber says, and this is the full quote of what I had began my comments today with: "How should the Tribunal treat a defendant whose health, while good enough to engage in the ordinary and non-strenuous activities of everyday life is not sufficiently robust to withstand all the rigours of trial work -- the late nights, the stressful cross-examinations, the courtroom confrontations -- unless the hearing is reduced to one day a week or even one day a month? Must the Trial Chamber be forced to choose between setting that defendant free and allowing the case to grind to an effective halt? In the Appeals Chamber's view, to ask that question is to answer it." To be clear, the Appeals Chamber made these comments in connection with the accused's right to self-representation and in light of the increased demands placed on the health of the accused by exercising that right. Nevertheless, the Prosecution submits that the analysis is applicable to this case as well. In this situation, should the Trial Chamber be forced to choose between setting Mr. Stanisic free and sitting only on days when Mr. Stanisic is physically capable of travelling to the Tribunal to attend court in person, when the workable alternative of a videolink is available? In the Prosecution's view, to ask that question is to answer it. We must be able to come up with an alternative to physical presence. If one examines one of the considerations of the Zigiranyirazo case, is the accused's ability to assess the credibility of witnesses. The Prosecution would submit that the Tribunal's now regular use of videolink testimony is a clear indication that judges are able to make important decisions of credibility and reliability by viewing the witnesses on a video monitor. It would seem that an accused would have the same capacity as judges to make similar assessments of credibility. If the feed sent to the detention unit was of the camera focused upon the witness instead of the roving cuts and pans that show all of us in this process, if the feed that was sent to Mr. Stanisic was confined to a view of the witnesses, he would have the same ability as the judges in assessing credibility of witnesses over the screen of a monitor. In fact, if you consider the reality of the participation that other accused have in their trial, it is reasonable to conclude that a system of videolink plus secure communications offices Mr. Stanisic's equal and arguably more effective participation in the proceedings. At present, most in-court consultations between the accused and their attorneys occur during the breaks. If Mr. Stanisic were able to contemporaneously communicate with his defence team via secure e-mail or instant messaging, he would be able to send and receive messages throughout the course of the examination any time that he saw fit. The Chamber could reach the view that in light of Mr. Stanisic's health, that helping him participate in the comfort of his room with toilet facilities close at hand, that in avoiding the extra time spent in travel and the increased access to his defence team that secure communications would give him, the Chamber could -- considering all of this, would justify the Chamber implementing a regime in which Mr. Stanisic has the capacity to participate in the trial via videolink even in the absence of his waiver of that right. The Chamber would have a basis for restricting the important right to be physically present at trial if it found that maintaining Mr. Stanisic's health and ensuring the predictable progress of this trial were in the words of the Milosevic Appeals Chamber, a sufficiently important objective. It is the Prosecution's position that such would constitute such grounds. I have discussed with the Chamber the technical and the legal possibility of establishing such a video conference link. Before I commit the Prosecutor, Mr. Brammertz, to a definitive position on such novel issues as this, I would ask for an opportunity to speak with him. I have tried since yesterday afternoon to confer with him on this novel issue and other issues related to developments in this case. He is currently at UN headquarters in meetings and I have been unable to speak with him. I expect that I will be able to speak with him later in the week or at the latest upon his return next Monday. After conferring with him, I will immediately inform the Chamber of the Prosecution's position regarding the establishment of creating a method of participation through videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Trial Chamber would not make a decision on this matter before you conferred with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not requesting that the Court delay its important work for me to do so and I have set out why I think it's technically and legally possible but it is a novel issue that I am somewhat reluctant to commit Mr. Brammertz to without having had an opportunity to speak with him. So if the Court deems it prudent to proceed, it would have to proceed without a formal position of the Prosecution until such time as I am able to speak with Mr. Brammertz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The last point the Chamber asked for our submissions on was since there has already been a finding of fitness, should we proceed went 7th of April when Stanisic will presumably be out of the detention unit hospital. In short, the Prosecution's position is that in light of Dr. de Man's report, the Chamber must satisfy itself that Dr. de Man's report does not impugn the conclusions it arrived at several weeks ago. It is our position that the Chamber may do this based on the report itself, in conjunction with the evidence the Chamber heard that is necessary -- heard from the hearing that is necessary to interpret Dr. de Man's report. Or, the Chamber can do so after a relatively short hearing in which Dr. de Man appears before the Chamber. So in essence, the Prosecution believes it is possible for the Chamber to commence the trial with the openings on the 7th of April. The Prosecution stands ready and willing to do that. But it would seem that prudent that the Chamber must make some finding with respect to the significance of Dr. de Man's report. Your Honour, with respect to some of the issues that I was unable to address earlier. With respect to Dr. Mimica, he spent about two and three quarter hours examining Mr. Stanisic. With respect to Ms. Najman, she had three days in which she spoke with Mr. Stanisic. And with respect to Dr. Smit, we know that she had two visits; I'm not sure of the duration of those -- to those two visits. With respect to the Simic case, the trial commenced on the 10th of September, 2001, and he pled guilty on the 15th of May, 2002. So in the period between September 2001 and to the plea in May 2002, he did participate in the trial via videolink. I'm sorry, Your Honour. From the 10th of September 2001 up and until the -- I'm sorry, excuse me, Your Honour, he participated via videolink in that trial in the period between the 11th of February 2002, and 15th of May, 2002. So a period of approximately three months. In conclusion, Your Honour, while yesterday's developments were unexpected, they should not disrupt the careful and considered approach the Trial Chamber has adopted in ensuring that all the rights of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic are meticulously guarded while we attempt to get this trial underway. The allegations in the indictment are grievous. The conditions of Mr. Stanisic which impedes our progress is at best a temporary condition. International justice cannot countenance its objectives being frustrated under these circumstances. It is incumbent upon all of us as participants in this trial to work together to find a way forward, a way that protects the rights of both accused and brings justice to the victims of the crimes charged. The Prosecution remains at the disposal of the Chamber in its continued efforts to move this case forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, the Defence for Mr. Stanisic will address the six options addressed by the honourable Trial Chamber. I myself will address the first option and the fourth, fifth and sixth option while my learned friend, Mr. Jordash will address the second and the third option. As a preliminary remark, we as Defence for Mr. Stanisic would like to stress that his current physical and medical mental situation prevents us from having received detailed and adequate instructions from the defendant. However, within the boundaries of our ethical codes, we believe that we are at liberty to engage in some legal discussions and raise some points of law, submissions on the fitness issue in order to assist the honourable Chamber in arriving at the justifiable conclusion. When it concerns, Your Honours, the first option, the severance, possibility for severance, our principal view as Defence team is that such a request or initiation for request should either come from the Prosecution or the Defence team from Mr. Simatovic, since predominantly his procedural rights, his procedural position in this case seem to be involved in the event of a need for severance due to medical reasons. Your Honours, apart from the time limit for an application for severance as set out in Rule 72(a) which could be met even after the expiry in the event of new information or circumstances, it might be instructive as a point of law to take into account the analogy with the case law as developed by the ICTY in the event of joint trials with co-indictees which were not yet in the custody of the court. There are two precedents, Dokmanovic, the ruling of 28 November, 1997, granting a motion for separation of trials on the grounds that none of the co-accused of that individual was at that time in the custody of the court, nor did it appear to be in the process of being transferred to the custody of the court. The Chamber in this case, Your Honours, considered the application of also Article 21, section 4 under C of the Statute guaranteeing the accused's right to be tried without undue delay. Also, the case law of the ICTR reveals a similar approach, holding that the element of avoiding undue delay and assuring the accused's right to a speedy trial may be seen as a factor for justification for an order of separation of trials. However, the fact that an accused's trial will be speedier if severance is granted, does not in itself constitute a reason for granting separation of trials as a point of law, when the co-accused is already in the custody or awaiting trial. Reference can be made to the decision of 25th September, 2006 in the Delalic case, decision on the motions for separation of trials filed by the accused Delalic and Mucic and I'll refer also to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... from that decision. I am asking whether what you just stated comes from that decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's a summary from the principal ruling of Delalic et al. In the instant case, we as Defence team for Mr. Stanisic, believe that it's primarily up to Your Honour's discretion to assess the applicability of this factor in specific with regard to the accused Mr. Simatovic, of course in the event of a substantial adjournment of the case of Mr. Stanisic is unavoidable. When it concerns, therefore, the first option, we, as Defence for Mr. Stanisic, leave the possibility for a potential severance in the hands of the Court believing that the primary initiative for such a request should either be the Prosecution or the Defence of Mr. Simatovic. My learned colleague Mr. Jordash will address the second and third option and I will return, Your Honours, with the fourth to the sixth option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In relation to the second and third options, clearly there is a degree of overlap and I hope you will forgive me if I deal in part with that overlap. It's our preference and we would put forward this approach that the number two option is the best option and the fairest option and the option which is likely to obtain an expeditious trial and one that can continue with the least interruption. We would submit that Dr. de Man's report, seen in conjunction with Dr. Falke and the treating psychiatrist at the UNDU clearly provides ample information which can satisfy the Trial Chamber that Mr. Stanisic is seriously unwell, but that there is a good chance, a very good chance, an expected chance that he will recover and we will return to the situation dealt with by Your Honours in the fitness decision of the 10th of March of this year. Presently, we have a huge amount of medical evidence and it's wrong, we would submit, that the report of Dr. de Man is seen in isolation from that medical evidence. I'm not going to clearly take Your Honours through it, but it must be seen in conjunction. It is the latest and it's the latest medical evidence and an indication of the deterioration of the medical condition. I would make the following observations: One, it's an independent evaluation, this is Dr. de Man's report, clearly not in any way swayed by any adversarial consideration. And secondly, it is medical evidence which, number one, stands alongside and has been arrived at through proper consultation with both Mr. McFadden and the medical staff from UNDU and in particular, Ms. Petrovic and Dr. Falke. And it's important to note that there is a concurrence of diagnosis between the treating psychiatrist and Dr. de Man. If Your Honours look at Dr. de Man's report at page 4 of the report, paragraph 3, I won't read it out but Your Honours will see that there is a concurrence of opinion considering the depth of the depression. Likewise, paragraph 5, there appears to be a concurrence in the view as to the appropriate treatment. There is no suggestion, we would submit, that Dr. de Man did not see the medical records. In fact, it would be rather strange to indicate on page 1 of the report that the accused had given permission to look at the medical records but then not to go on to actually peruse them. In any event, whether the medical records were seen or not, Dr. de Man consulted with the treating psychiatrist, so we can be fairly confident that Dr. de Man had access to the relevant details of Mr. Stanisic's mental illness or mental condition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, why did you submit that Dr. de Man did not see the medical records when he had asked for the medical records and had been given permission to view them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, it seems that he doesn't mention anything from the medical records, as well as there seems to be some incorrect information regarding the birth date and place of Mr. Stanisic, which is correctly reported in the medical records. So we don't have a clear, affirmative indication of that but there seems to be implicit in his report the fact that he did not have the access that he required of those medical records.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, looking at the paragraph just below the title report, it's quite clear that this doctor, Dr. de Man, obtained information from Mr. McFadden, obtained information from Ms. Petrovic, and thereafter, appears to say obtained permission from Mr. Stanisic for the medical file and gave permission for additional questions to be put to the medical officer, Dr. Falke. It's a detailed report, we would submit. It's consistent with the latest report from -- well, relatively consistent with the latest reports from Dr. Falke and I'll come to those in a moment. It's certainly consistent with way in which the medical condition appears to have been developing since the 14th of March, 2008, shortly after Your Honours' decision. But Your Honours will see in relation to page 4 of the report, the DSM-IV classification is referred to. I personally didn't know exactly what that referred to so I obtained from the internet what this classification meant. In particular, in relation to the GAF score of 21 to 30, the Global Assessment of Functioning scale, and I handed up copies of what these scales mean to your learned's legal officer, and I don't intend to refer to all of the comments, but I would particularly refer Your Honours to the 21 to 30 score, GAF axis 5 which is relevant, we would say, to a consideration of almost all the options Your Honours are considering, particularly of videolinks and the idea of starting within a week, that Dr. de Man's report would seem to suggest that there is a great deal of reason, of many reasons to be somewhat cautious of the trial starting in any form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just point us again to the relevant section.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If Your Honour would look at the actual report from Dr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution have this?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a copy to them. But I'm particularly referring to axis 5 GAF, Global Assessment of Functioning scale, score 21 to 30, which one, suggests that Dr. de Man took his task very seriously and actually went and used proper diagnostic tools but secondly, the actual result is a cause of concern, particularly when considering whether the trial could stand in the very near future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you are inviting us to look at the second -- at the document headed "Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) scale."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And 21 to 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Behaviour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: "Behaviour is considerably influenced by delusions or hallucinations or serious impairment in communication or judgement."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. We would say that that clearly impacts upon a consideration of whether the trial should start in any form at present but also indicates this is a psychiatrist, a neuropsychiatrist, at that, who took his task extremely seriously and approached it with some depth. The issue of opening up another --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, just help me with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- GAF scale. It starts at zero and it goes up to 91 to 100. So is this a gradation or a scale of the gravity of the illness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It would appear to be a scale of -- indicating the gravity of the impairment, yes. Impairment in functioning, according to -- sorry, I beg your pardon. It appears to be the consideration of the client's psychological, social and occupational functioning on a hypothetical continuum of medical health illness - I'm reading from the title of the top - which does not include impairment of functioning due to physical or environmental limitations. Which would be of course consistent, if Your Honours go back to the report, Dr. de Man's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does it proceed from the worst to the better, from zero to 91 to 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 91 to 100 is superior functioning down to the bottom which would appear to be -- appear to deal with a serious suicidal act, so less suicidal risk or suicidal act to the most grave dealt with 1 to 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In our submission, there is plenty of evidence given the way in which that report was compiled and the consultations which were taken during the compilation. In relation to number three, we would submit it would be medically inappropriate and unhelpful from the standpoint of an expeditious trial to launch forward into more examinations, and I particularly refer Your Honours to the medical evidence which has emerged from Dr. Falke since Your Honour's decision on the 10th of March, 2008. In particular, the letter of the 14th of March, 2008 in which Dr. Falke noted at paragraph 3 one of the factors which has led to a deterioration was the stress caused by scrutiny into health over the past few weeks. This was echoed again by Dr. Falke on the 17th of March who noted again that the constant medical examinations are causing a deterioration or at least a factor in the deterioration. And interestingly and significantly noting that Rule 34(b) of the Rules of Detention were certainly in Dr. Falke's mind in terms of the conflicts being created in terms of carrying out the investigations for the Court and at the same time being the treating doctor. And again, on the 28th of March, 2008, Dr. Falke, in the letter there to the Registrar makes exactly the same point. So we would submit that there must come a time when the medical condition which has to be considered as absolutely paramount, and this is the time. And in particular, this is the time because there is a remedy and according to the latest evidence from the treating doctors and Dr. de Man, this is a situation which will improve and which will be remedied. And we would submit in those circumstances, the medical situation should be given absolute paramount significance knowing that we can be back into court between three to six months back to the position of the 10th of March, 2008 decision that Mr. Stanisic is fit. We don't seek to reiterate those arguments on the current available evidence. The current available evidence suggests give Mr. Stanisic a period of time on the treatment as suggested and he will be ready for trial in three to six months. If I may just finally deal with the suggestion that Mr. Stanisic has already been receiving this treatment. In my submission, that is not borne out from Dr. de Man's statement which indicates on page 4, the final paragraph, there is a recommendation that Mr. Stanisic receives immediate treatment with tricyclic anti-depressants. And again, I reiterate, and if Your Honours turn over the page to the last page of the report, Your Honours will see that Dr. de Man consulted with Petrovic concerning the medication and then the recommendation of this new treatment was agreed upon between the two of them. So we are in a new situation with new diagnosis and a new drug with a hope and a real possibility of being well in three to six months. In my submission, that should be given proper due consideration. We are not, in our submission, at the point where we need to consider the more drastic solutions. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is your comment on the impact such a postponement might have on the right of Simatovic to a fair and expeditious trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to comment without knowing exactly what their position is. It could impact insofar as there is a further delay, so of course there is some impact. But as my learned friends from the Prosecution indicated when considering -- right at the outset of their submissions, we are talking of only a relatively short delay, a short delay which could, with Your Honours' leave, be dealt with on provisional release, and it may well be that the accused Simatovic does not oppose such a delay, especially if the delay actually prevents a further delay in the future, and we would submit that is likely to be the case. If he is well now before we start, there is likely to be less delay during the trial, in fact we could have a quicker and more efficient trial which would benefit both accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All of this of course is derived from Dr. de Man's report. The Prosecutor says it doesn't stand up to scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's derived from Dr. de Man's report which itself is derived from consultation with the treating psychiatrist. In our submission, there can be no more knowledgeable medical expert at this point other than returning to the fitness issue concerning Mr. Stanisic's present condition, there's Dr. Petrovic, who is most familiar with Mr. Stanisic's condition, and Dr. de Man consulted with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say about the Prosecutor's suggestion that Dr. de Man might be brought to the Court for a limited examination, limited hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We -- may I just take instructions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We wouldn't oppose such a suggestion. We don't think it's strictly necessary given the thrust and tenure of the various reports since we've had the fitness decision but we wouldn't oppose that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would like now to make some submissions on the fourth suggested option, the videolink, and we would submit there are three arguments not to follow that option. In the first place, such participation would not change the current disabilities of the accused to participate in such a videolink trial on the basis of his current situation as set out by Dr. de Man. In light of the, in our view, clear reports of both Dr. Falke and Dr. de Man, return of the accused to the detention centre and the start of the case while he participates through videolink is, in our humble view, not realistic. I noted, though, that the Prosecution agrees, acknowledges, that the report of Dr. de Man and also supported by Ms. Petrovic, a new element which was not available at Your Honours' decision of the 10th of March, 2008, where Your Honours in paragraph 39 of the decision held that none of the experts in that time detected any psychosis and both experts, Dr. de Man, and the treating psychiatrist, have now concurred in this view that there is a situation of psychotic features. So there is merit in the argument that a trial, through videolink, in this stage is, in this situation, not realistic. The participation akin to magnitude of the case at hand presupposes of course that the accused may participate through such a videolink, otherwise we submit substitution of the physical presence of the accused in the courtroom is of no value. We do not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why do you say that? Dr. de Man says there are no signs of any cognitive deterioration which would suggest that he's in a position, he would be in a position to understand the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That's indeed a valid observation, Your Honour. I'm not in a position to comment on the differentiation between having cognitive capabilities on the one hand and having psychotic features on the other hand. I simply observe that we encounter a new situation in that there is something additional to the medical evidence which was brought before Your Honours which led to the decision of the 10th of March. As a layperson, I can only say that it seems to me quite difficult but for that we could have to indeed invite Dr. de Man or other experts to find out whether somebody with these kind of features is able to participate through a video conference but still, you have the problem that the absence of a physical ability to stand trial of course will also affect the ability to participate through videolink. And of course we don't contest the existence of any technical developments and equipment nowadays to ensure such a trial by videolink. However, it requires, and it is predominant for ensuring those -- that equipment to be in place that the defendant, of course, has the technical skills and abilities to make use of them. The Prosecution refers to computer access, e-mail access. All of this, of course, requires presence, basic presence of knowledge and also capacities of the accused to clearly make use of that modern technology. There is a second reason, Your Honours, we submit, why we believe that the video conference is not the most viable option. We submit that legally, legally it equates a trial in absentia. For this, we rely on the case which was brought before the Appeals Chamber judgement in the judgement on the request of the Republic of Croatia for review of the decision of the Trial Chamber II of 18th of July, 1997 and other decisions. Interestingly, Your Honours, in paragraph 59 of that Appeals Chamber judgement, it's been noted by the Appeals Judges that even when the accused has clearly waived his right to be tried in his physical presence, it would prove extremely difficult or even impossible for an international criminal court to determine the innocence or guilt of that accused. As Your Honours know, only for the so-called incidental jurisdiction of the court or ancillary jurisdiction of the court, the Appeals Chamber left albeit with an exceptional possibility, a trial in absentia open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just remind us of the context of that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That context related to a content of court proceedings due to the refusal to obey one of the orders issued by the Court and although we are mindful that the context is indeed quite different, we believe that this principle as set out in paragraph 59 of the Court's decision is applicable in the instant case. We believe there is a second precedent, and of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did the question arise in that case?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Because there was a refusal to comply with the request of the Court to produce evidence to the Court on part of some of the officials of Croatia and I believe that the Court held that binding orders can only be administered against governments, institutions and only individuals can be subjected to subpoenas. That was the essence of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was anybody being tried in absentia --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No, as a result of the refusal to comply with the subpoena of the court, contempt of court proceedings were initiated against an individual and in that situation the Court held - and I believe it was unanimous - that only in such a situation, one could deviate from the primary jurisdiction principles of the court, namely the trial not in absentia. But our point is that the decision of the Appeals Chamber also eludes to the availability of a waiver, that even in the event of a waiver, it is difficult to understand how a trial could take place without the physical presence of the accused. And the Prosecution, I think, rightfully pointed to the second precedent in this regard, the interlocutory appeals decision of 30 October 2006 in the case of the Prosecutor versus Zigiranyirazo, the ICTR Appeals Chamber judgement. This authority, Your Honours, is maybe more proper than the decision referred to by the Prosecution in the Milosevic case because the Appeals Chamber decision in Milosevic was followed by this decision and notably in footnote 31, 51 and 52, the Appeals Chamber refers to the Milosevic decision. Still it came to the conclusion that the modality to have a trial, at least a part of a trial through videolink violated the rights of the accused and the Appeals Chamber held that the Trial Chamber erred in law in holding that this right could be met by videolink. As Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because it was not the least restrictive measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is not a decision that says that in principle, a videolink can't be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, it's not an absolute right that the accused should be tried in his physical presence, but if Your Honours would look to paragraph 21 of that decision, the Appeals Chamber notes that the appellant's sense of being wronged in such circumstances is well understandable. As the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber noted, Mr. Bagaragaza's testimony did not cover simply background information or matter other than the acts and conduct of the accused. According to the Prosecution's own statement and the Trial Chamber's consideration, the witness was a key Prosecutor witness against the appellant. Based on the foregoing, the Trial Chamber's restrictions were unwarranted and excessive in these circumstances and failed the test of proportionality." Of course it's difficult now to project this ruling on the whole case of Mr. Stanisic but we can observe that there are numerous witnesses in this case which will provide your Chamber with more than simple background information as eluded to by the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 21. And although we submit indeed it does not exclude absolutely the trial by videolink, one should contextualise this in also the importance of the charges, the severity of the charges and the evidence which the Prosecution intends to lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, we are beyond the time for the break so we'll take a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just rounding up the fourth option, the videolink option, Your Honour. Your Honours did address me some questions on the Zigiranyirazo decision and it may be brought to the attention of the Court that the situation at hand, similar to the Zigiranyirazo decision, is unprecedented. In paragraph 21, the Appeals Chamber observes that such a procedure over an accused's objection is unprecedented before the Tribunal and before the ICTY. Interestingly, in footnote 41 of the Appeals Chamber's decision, the Appeals Chamber refers to the Simic case as a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in paragraph 21 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Paragraph 12. Paragraph 12, you find the observation of the Appeals Chamber that such a procedure over an accused's objection is unprecedented before the Tribunal and before the ICTY. And footnote 41 refers to the mentioned Simic case. What is particularly instructive, we submit for Your Honours, is that the Trial Chamber expressly note that not only Simic concerned in sentencing hearing therefore not a determination of guilt or innocence as such --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that was clarified. It covered both.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Both -- I think he had the use of the video conference link for a certain part of the trial as well as the sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That is indeed noted by the Appeals Chamber. But what is particularly additional of interest, Your Honour, is that the Chamber notes that Mr. Simic filed a total of 25 waivers of his right to be present in court. And in our humble submission, this is, of course, not without reason cited by the Appeals Chamber in footnote 41. Secondly, Your Honour, you may see that in the same paragraph 12 of the Appeals Chamber decision, the Court, Appeals Chamber clearly holds that participation via videolink is not considered presence, therefore it's our submission as mentioned that a procedure via videolink should be equated with a trial in absentia. And my last observation from this Appeals Chamber ruling, Your Honours, relates to the paragraph 14 of this ruling where, although the Appeals Chamber acknowledges that this right to be physically present is not absolute, the Appeals Chamber only accepts an exception for the situation as described in Rule 80(b) removing an accused for disruptive behaviour. We submit that none of those ingredients are applicable here and because of the unprecedented character of this fourth option as suggested, we believe there is no legal basis to have a full trial against Mr. Stanisic based on a videolink. I believe this was Your Honour's questions to the Defence, whether we believe that the trial without any exception, trial as such is warranted by law is able to be based on the current law or the jurisprudence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 12, this same sentence to which you referred, the Appeals Chamber observes that such a procedure ..." Do you see the word "initially"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It perhaps has a significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. I agree, Your Honour. But I agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it means that this is a statement which the Appeals Chamber is making at this stage of the -- of its writing of the judgement; but later on it develops arguments that show, in my view, that in some circumstances, the videolink can be used over the objection of the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we as Defence agree with Your Honour's interpretation of the decision with two remarks. First of all, we still believe that the Appeals Chamber is willing to accept any exception to this principal rule, and the lack of any express provisions in the Statute, paragraph 12 refers to that, only if the stage of exceptional circumstances have been met, and we believe that that stage has not yet arrived in this instant case, apart from the medical ability or physical ability of an accused to participate via videolink. We still believe that the Appeals Chamber only allows such an exception in very specific and restricted conditions and circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you say that we haven't yet reached a stage where recourse to this exceptional procedure is warranted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: It is, of course, with ultimum remedium, you could say in legal terms, which should be administered with great caution if the Court is willing to go beyond as set forth by the Appeals Chamber decision in this judgement, we still believe that going beyond should be restricted to very limited circumstances, and I cannot imagine that the Appeals Chamber had in mind that a full trial will be conducted through videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I go back, though, to the preference which Mr. Jordash expressed for the second option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is, three to six months down the road we would commence the trial. But that proceeds on the basis that a view is taken that the accused would be well enough then. I mean what allows us to be sanguine about that possibility. Why should we be confident, Mr. Jordash, that in three to six months' time the accused would be well enough to attend court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if you ask the Defence to come with a clear and equivocal answer, we would say the only person who could answer that question will be Dr. de Man because he made this estimation. And it could be helpful, Your Honours, if the Court is willing to go into the suggestion of the Prosecution to hear Dr. de Man about the report is how his -- this term of at least three to six months is determined by him, whether it's based on experience or whether it's based on any diagnosis. Currently, Your Honours, we -- as Defence, we have to deal with the documents we have and if this expert's diagnosis is that Mr. Stanisic will be able to attend trial physically in a normal manner, within three to six months, of course nobody will again give the guarantee that something can happen within that time-frame, but this is of course now the starting point of our legal submissions of today. And if -- having this in mind, we believe that it would be actually a premature exhaustion of the remedies such as videolink conference or trial while not having awaited the opportunity for the recovery as indicated by Dr. de Man. So we are saying that the Appeals Chamber judgement, although it may allow for exceptions to the rule, still requires that the test of proportionality will be met. And in our view, the proportionality has not yet been met since the option of Dr. de Man has not yet been exhausted. So therefore, we believe that starting a trial by videolink in this stage would violate the test of proportionality as envisioned by the Appeals Chamber. Your Honour, my learned friend, Mr. Jordash, rightly points to the fact that of course the only thing we as Defence were informed of that, and that's also the starting point of Your Honour's, that Mr. Stanisic - and this was I believe the basis of your decision of the 10th of March - needs psychotherapy, yet it was never determined by any specialist until so far for how long this treatment, the therapy, would have to last for the recovery. And I believe that even Dr. Smit, the court-appointed expert, during testimony couldn't give a clear estimation or indication as to the time-frame. So actually this is the first indication, clear indication from an expert about the time-frame. That's where we are. And therefore, we believe, in all modesty, that it's quite premature now to say that all our avenues have been exhausted so let's start with a trial by videolink while there is a possibility for this recovery although we agree with Your Honours that we cannot give, as Defence, apart from being lay persons, any guarantee that indeed this recovery will be concluded within three to six months. But this is the course the best evidence we have. Dr. de Man's report is currently the best evidence we have and therefore, we think in all honesty that it would go against the rationale of the Appeals Chamber decision of 2006 by saying that while this right to be present is not absolute, the videolink option is not ruled out by the Court in that case while knowing that we have another avenue, namely recovery of the accused, to ensure that he can be physically present. And we believe that the case law at this moment, as also set forth by the Appeals Chamber, is in our favour in that also the reference to the national jurisdictions, the Supreme Court of the United States cases, the Crosby case of 1993, clearly give preference to the physical presence of the accused person. Now, if Your Honours allow me, I will round up with the fifth and the sixth options that Your Honours have suggested to the Defence team. Of course in light of my observations just a moment ago, I still believe that if Mr. Stanisic would return to the detention centre on the 7th of April, in light of the medical evidence, the best evidence we have now, the report of Dr. de Man supported by Dr. Petrovic, we still do not have the recovery of this accused person. Therefore, as to the fourth option, we believe that this is not a viable option. The additional question, Your Honours presented to also the Defence team also goes to the decision, which was not previously mentioned in this courtroom this afternoon, by the Appeals Chamber of the ICTR presided by Justice Pocar in Prosecution versus Nzirorera, the ICTR Appeals Chamber of 5th October, 2007. Quite recently one can say very shortly, Your Honour, the appellant on a certain day in June 2007 was ill and the medical doctor pronounced him unfit to attend trial for three days. Counsel requested the Chamber to adjourn the proceedings until the appellant would be medically fit. The Chamber denied the request and held that it would proceed with cross-examination of a Prosecution witness in relation to the case of a co-accused, so it did not even deal with the case against the appellant himself. In short, the Appeals Chamber reversed its decision holding that despite the presence of appellant's counsel, and I specifically refer to paragraph 11 of this Appeals Chamber decision, and although noting that the right to be physically present is not absolute, the proportionality test was not met in that case and there are four interesting observations, very shortly, the Chamber gives in paragraph 15. First, it considered that the circumstances of that case were complex and lengthy. The Appeals Chamber was not satisfied that the three-day delay to the trial was sufficiently to outweigh the statutory right of the appellant to be present because it was no fault of his own. Secondly, the reliance by the Chamber on Rule 92 bis and 94(b) was in view of the Chamber misguided.
