And thirdly, the Court held it is irrelevant for these purposes whether or not the cross-examination of a witness has been conducted in the case against a co-accused or against the accused, the appellant himself. It was also not relevant, the Chamber held, whether the witness's testimony was likely to concern the alleged acts and conduct of the co-accused only. The Chamber's restrictions on the appellant's fair trial rights were unwarranted and excessive and this failed the proportionality test and therefore, the appeal request was granted from Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, that the Appeals Chamber was not satisfied that the three-day delay to the trial was sufficient to outweigh the statutory right of the appellant because it was no fault of his own but might a three-month delay or a six-month delay be sufficient to outweigh that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, it is very dangerous to make a determination whether three days are sufficient, a week, two weeks. Where is where we draw the line? Our submission is that the principal line is that when there are other avenues which are still open, those should be followed before going into other options. And it's not up to us as Defence team to say whether, in this case, a delay of three --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What precisely do you say that is the other avenue that's open to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: The other avenue is that the Court considers the possibility or at least gives the possibility for this avenue suggested by Dr. de Man, namely that with a thorough therapy, between three and six months, and maybe on a permanent basis outside the detention centre, because let's face it, the detention centre is, of course, not a hospital and although we have no doubt as to the, of course, the good faith of the medical officers there, it is of course difficult for the detention centre to have a patient there treated on a permanent basis. Therefore, in our humble submission, the other avenue is the avenue which has been offered by Dr. de Man, namely a period of structural -- structural period of treatment. Actually, we're not going back to the fitness issue but Your Honours clearly had in mind when rendering the fitness ruling on the 10th of March, that Mr. Stanisic would undergo a form of psychotherapy and reading the report of Dr. de Man, it seems to us that this is right now the only avenue which is there to make him recover and make him at the least physically fit to attend trial. So this is actually also why my learned friend, Mr. Jordash, elaborated on the second option we believe is in the best interests of justice in this stage of the proceedings. May I briefly and as by way of last remark, Your Honour, refer to the fact that the reliance by the Prosecution on the jurisprudence of the Special Court for Sierra Leone in the Sesay case clearly is not suitable precedent, we believe. We submit that in the Sesay case, and indeed Mr. Jordash is lead counsel in that case, one dealt with a refusal to appear. We are dealing here with considering the information as we have received it until now, an absence due to medical reasons. And also the Trial Chamber decision in the Bagaragaza case of the 2nd November, 2000, in paragraph 5 and 6 refers to the fact that Mr. Bagaragaza chose not to appear which are two totally different situations as in the current situation. There are of course other precedents to mention therefore we submitted this human rights report to Your Honours, a report of 17th November, 2006. Not that we suggest that human rights, as such, may be a legal authority but the interesting part of this report, Your Honours, is that it gives a brief summary of all the international, national case law, human rights case law, and it also refers to the discussions which preceded Article 63 of the ICC Statute. The Rome Statutes follows a similar approach --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Tell us, what is the source? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: It's a Human Rights Watch report of the 17th of November, 2006. We have distributed copies to Your Honours and amongst the participants today. Interestingly, I mentioned the Crosby case of the United States in 1993 is mentioned there. But the interesting part of it is that preceding Article 63 of the ICC Statute, there were three competing perspectives on trials in absentia. And interestingly, the first perspective, namely an exclusion, total exclusion of trials in absentia was the prevailing view. Interestingly, also the United Nations Secretary's report on the establishment of the ICTY, it's my last authority, and the Statute report of the 3rd May, 1993, and the Secretary-General of the United Nations, I quote, he comments as follows: "A trial should not commence until the accused is physically present before the International Tribunal." This was a report which lies at the heart of this Honourable Tribunal and we respectfully submit that also in light of the situation which the accused envisions, namely -- and Your Honours may recall that the Prosecution, during his provisional release hearings announced to seek for life imprisonment of Mr. Stanisic. Now we believe in all honesty and modesty that one cannot commence a trial where a defendant who may be facing life imprisonment without him being physically present and therefore we agree in this regard that the Human Rights Watch report, in our view, reflects the answers to your questions four and five you asked us to comment on. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, Franko Simatovic's Defence is now in a position to state their opinion and partly accept the argument provided by the Prosecution and partly by the Defence. I'm not going to go over the same ground, I'm just going to state the facts. In a situation that we are now facing, and that is to discuss the possibilities of a trial, this situation has arisen from the opinion of the psychiatrist de Man. We are not in a position to argue with his findings because in the previous part of the proceedings, we heard other evidence and we heard other witnesses and also Stanisic's Defence obviously has immediate contact with their client and immediate insight into his health condition and we, as the Defence, accept the position as such and we will provide our position on the assumption that the Trial Chamber will accept it, together with the recommendations that were provided by Mr. de Man, the psychiatrist, and especially this refers to the deadlines, i.e., to the possibility for Mr. Stanisic's health to deteriorate. The first question that has been raised is the issue of the severance in keeping with Rule 82. The two criteria which have been provided for by Rule 82, the first one is the possible conflict of interest and the interests of justice which would lead to the decision on severing the cases. On the face of it, one might say that there might be a conflict of interest given the situation and that is that the interests of Mr. Stanisic is not to be tried in view of his health condition. On the other hand, there is also the interests of the accused Simatovic and that is to have the right to an expeditious trial to be met. However, the right to a fair trial is an overriding right and the right is on the side of Mr. Simatovic. Our position is that only a joint trial, in view of the circumstances, one could indeed speak of a fair trial. Whether there is an infringement of the right to expeditious trial if this trial is delayed in view of the time scale envisaged by Dr. de Man who spoke about the possibility of Mr. Stanisic's health to improve, we have to say that we only partly agree with the Prosecutor and we believe that the right of the accused would not be infringed when it comes to an expeditious trial. In view of that, the Defence can say that unlike the position of the Prosecution that have provided their opinion, and in view of the circumstance that Mr. Simatovic has been detained for two months and that he could spend another six months in detention and that the eight months in pre-trial should not mean the infringement of his rights to an expeditious trial. We believe that all possible consequences would be removed if our client was provisionally released. This is not that we propose as a condition, but as a possibility. This is going to be the subject of a special ruling of the Chamber as a result of a special hearing. The Defence would like to draw everybody's attention to the fact, which has already been done, that the indictment was issued on the 1st of May, 2003, and that these proceedings have already been ongoing for five years and that the right to an expeditious trial has been an issue that is long overdue. But there is also an obligation to take into all the other circumstances that have a bearing on the trial and these are the circumstances that concern the work of the Prosecutor's office and the Tribunal as a whole, and taking into account that these are very complicated trials that will necessitate long trials. However, when it comes to the infringement of the right to an expeditious trial, this has been removed by the fact that Mr. Simatovic was already on provisional release. The Defence agrees with the Prosecution in their position that all the recommendations that exist at this moment and especially the recommendations by Dr. de Man are based on a possible unfitness for trial of Mr. Stanisic is of a temporary nature. And this Defence believes that for as long as there is a possibility for a joint trial to continue and the findings of Dr. de Man indicates such a possibility, the Defence believes that this is the avenue that should be explored, i.e., that joint trials should be supported. Obviously there are circumstances that might exclude such a possibility, but I believe that at this point, we are in a situation where we can still reckon with such a possibility. I would like to remind everybody that the counts against the accused Stanisic and Simatovic are identical and that they apply to the same extent to the both accused, that all the evidence that the Prosecution has proposed is similar for both accused. In their work, the Defence has followed the suggestions of the pre-trial judge from one of the previous pre-trial Status Conferences. The Defence has cooperated in order to avoid overlapping and with a view to the most expeditious trial. The Defence has decided to propose two joint expert opinions in this -- these proceedings so all these circumstances are not in favour of the severance of the cases and I believe that this, at this moment is more important than the right to the accused of an expeditious trial in case there is a postponement within the deadlines mentioned by Dr. de Man and which were recommended by him as the time needed for Mr. Stanisic's recovery. This Defence believes that a decision on severance would be premature because there is still a fair chance that a joint trial may be conducted and that a decision on severance would not be the right decision at this moment. This also implies that the Defence is inclined to believe and considers that a possible postponement of trial within the time-frames recommended by Dr. de Man, should the trial accept that recommendation, is acceptable and we believe that it would not infringe our client's right to an expeditious trial. Whether the postponement will also mean that the case will have to go back to a pre-trial phase and will have to be referred to a pre-trial judge or whether another option will be considered, that will also require an additional report on Mr. Stanisic's health within shorter deadlines, this Defence believes that it is up to the organisation of the work of this Tribunal and is not in a position to provide any suggestions along these lines. As far as possible medical examinations and evaluations of Mr. Stanisic's health and his fitness for trial are concerned, at this moment, the Defence can only rely on the last report provided by the psychiatrist and we are not in a position to provide any evaluation for the reasons that I've already mentioned and those are that most of the proceedings that preceded this moment during which the -- Mr. Stanisic's fitness for trial has been evaluated has always been done in an ex parte form. In keeping with all of that, I believe that the Defence of the accused Simatovic is not in a position to provide any comments to Mr. Stanisic's fitness for trial via videolink and in that sense we accept the arguments that were provided by the Defence of Mr. Stanisic. As for the possible trial based on the decision that was previously passed in view of Mr. Stanisic's fitness for trial, the Defence believes that Dr. de Man's report is of crucial importance on any position and that the Trial Chamber should reach a decision whether they accept Dr. de Man's position or not; and should they not accept it, it would be only then that the possibilities could be considered, and these possibilities would arise from the previously-reached decisions by way of which the Trial Chamber has decided that Mr. Stanisic is fit for trial. The conclusion of the Defence of the Accused Simatovic is that at this moment, the only adequate solution would be to postpone the trial by the time that the Trial Chamber deems appropriate. And once Mr. Stanisic is reexamined, and once his ability for trial is reexamined, then we should embark on further considerations of possible forms of trial unless Mr. Stanisic's health deteriorates. If his health improves, however, the way Dr. de Man has envisaged, then it would be a short period of time which is acceptable by the Defence of the Accused Simatovic as a delay and we believe that his interest would not be impaired. In addition to filing an application for provisional release for the Accused Simatovic, the Defence would also like to point to the fact that in the course of February, March, up to the 1st of February, the Prosecution has disclosed lots of documents and that the possible postponement would be made -- put to good use for the preparation of Mr. Simatovic's Defence. The Defence believes that Mr. Simatovic could do that while provisionally released but as I've already said, this will be the subject of separate considerations by the Trial Chamber. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Groome, would you pay particular attention in your reply to the Defence argument that while there may be derogations from the fundamental right of an accused to be present in court, in this case, the institution of video conference link would be disproportionate because the Trial Chamber would not have exhausted all other avenues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before I do that, if it is acceptable to the Court, there are a few other matters I would like to just respond to. The first one is the Global Assessment of Functioning, or the GAF scale. If the Court would take a look at that document again, I note that at the top of the first paragraph, the last sentence of that first paragraph states that the assessment is of the client's functioning during the previous 12 months. So this determination or setting or characterisation of Mr. Stanisic's mental state is not simply of an isolated day but of a 12-month period. I say that because if the Court recalls, none of the other experts that testified at the trial -- at the hearing described the symptoms that are described in this range of 21 to 30. And in fact, Dr. Mimica, if the Court recalls from his report, his assessment of Mr. Stanisic over a 12-month period was a 65. And also he made a finding that his present, at the time that he examined him, it was actually a 70. So according to Dr. Mimica, there had actually been an improvement on this scale. When one considers why would there be such a dramatic drop in this scale, is it a deterioration, or is it simply that all that's required to create that kind of precipitous drop would be the self-reporting of a single symptom. If the Court looks at 21 to 30, it's phrased in the disjunctive, it's "or ." So just simply one of those symptoms reported by an examinee could lead to a considerable drop and a symptom that I suggest to the Court is simply Mr. Stanisic self-reporting that he has had a hallucination. I would also point out, and I believe it's clear from Dr. Mimica's testimony and his report, that this is simply a clinical aid. It is not a replacement for the overall diagnosis, and I believe that my -- the Defence of Mr. Stanisic is actually placing greater weight on this -- greater significance on this finding of de Man regarding the characterisation on a scale of 21 to 30 than is really warranted. The second thing that I would like to address is with respect to the video conferencing, whether Mr. Knoops raised the possibility that maybe Mr. Stanisic is not sufficiently technically equipped to deal with the technology of a computer. I must say I find that quite difficult to believe given that he was the head administrator of a large state security service in the 1990s during the computer age. But even if let's say that is the case, in my conversation with Mr. Falces this morning, I put to him the question if Mr. Stanisic were to be unable to -- if he's unable to type, there is currently now available on the market a tablet PC that operates simply as a note pad that someone with a stylus provided with this computer tablet can simply write notes as if they would write a note in court here and pass it to counsel. So even if the event that Mr. Stanisic does have some deficiencies in computer skills, accommodations could be made according to Mr. Falces that he would ensure that he would have the ability to effectively communicate with his counsel. Your Honour, could I ask for just a minute to confer with my colleagues with respect to the Court's request that I deal with the derogation and whether it's the last result?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will just be a minute. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to which is the greater derogation, and the argument could be made that if the Court accepts my evaluation of what is possible with a videolink, the fact that Mr. Stanisic could have contemporaneous, instantaneous conversation with his counsel throughout, it may in fact be viewed in fact less of a derogation of his ability to participate in a trial as opposed to what's being recommended, that we adjourn for a period of three to six months. I think another way to look at this is if we were to set up a room, let's say, in this courtroom that could accommodate Mr. Stanisic's particular medical needs, he could sit there and he would be physically present but he would still have no greater capacity to participate in the trial than he would have if he were viewing that from the comfort of his own detention facility. I don't believe that the Court must adjourn this case for any considerable period of time before it is able to make a determination that it is appropriate that a substantial objective is achieved by employing a system of video conferencing on those days when Mr. Stanisic is physically unwell enough to make the trip to the court to be here in person. Many of the cases that we have referred to, particularly those ones dealing with trial in absentia are really dealing with the -- with circumstances in which the accused has absolutely no participation whatsoever. Here we are talking about what is -- or what's being proposed is a situation in which Mr. Stanisic would have equal or greater participation, the only difference would be that rather than viewing the witnesses in person, he would be viewing them over a video monitor. One thing that I did not mention in my initial remarks, but the capacity is also there that it would be a two-way videolink, so any time that Mr. Stanisic wants to address the Chamber, he could simply indicate that to his counsel, they could inform the Court, and then we could be looking at Mr. Stanisic in his cell addressing the Chamber directly on any point that he wishes to do so. So again, it's difficult for me to imagine how this incapacitates his participation and in fact I think it facilitates his participation. Have I addressed the concern of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You anticipate that Mr. Stanisic, from his cell, could address the Chamber directly?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So with respect to my discussions with Mr. Falces on his computer monitor could be mounted what is commonly referred to as a webcam so any time that he wanted to address the Chamber, if he indicated that to his attorney, of course we would not have the webcam on all of the time because that would infringe on his privacy if he's some how either using the toilet or something else, but any time that he wants to address the Court, he would be able to do so immediately from his cell. He would have that capacity in short order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I've satisfied the Chamber's question to me initially, I have no further comments to make, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. I thank the parties for their submissions. Mr. Knoops, you wanted to have another bite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, only maybe as a closing remark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: -- that with all due respect for the answer the Prosecution gave to the Chamber it, at least from our perspective, will still be a fundamental derogation without any fault or part of Mr. Stanisic. It's not about the technology, the abilities, the state of the art to have access to computers and to use computers. This is about whether the situation at hand justifies the conclusion that all alternative avenues have been explored for this principal derogation, this unprecedented derogation the Appeals Chamber alludes to. This is, I think, the key issue. And in all honesty, we not say that in this stage with this deep depression, with all due respect, the defendant can participant through videolink, have access and make access and use all of those state of the art equipment as envisioned by the Prosecution: This is in our view and our submission, the principal point. We therefore, we did stress -- we didn't reach that stage yet for determining whether a videolink is an alternative avenue at this stage. We're still, in our view, in the proceeding stage, namely the situation whether, due to the medical situation, Mr. Stanisic can participate or not. Thank you. Yes, my honourable learned friend, Mr. Jordash, refers that from this perspective, it's the first delay, it's not the third delay. Your Honours have now the timetable from Dr. de Man. If that timetable is not to be met for some reason or the other, then of course there is a new reason, there is a second delay and that may justify another determination of the videolink option. But we think that it's rather premature now in this stage to conclude that videolink fits within the alternative venues as the Chamber has in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But what do you mean when you say this is the first delay? What is the first delay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, the first delay in terms of Your Honours have now for the first time a picture of the timeframe for the recovery. Your Honours, until now, have not heard from any expert in this courtroom, nor the Prosecution experts, nor the Defence experts, nor the Court experts what is exactly now the prospect for recovery. I think that Dr. de Man is the first expert out of the whole series of experts that we have heard who comes to the concrete estimation in terms of time, when it's realistic that this individual can be physically present. This is what we mean with the first delay. In other words, if that time-frame, I believe it was Your Honour's question just a moment ago whether we believe that this time-frame can be met, this time-frame of three to six months, whether that's a viable time-frame, if that time-frame for one or the other reason could not be met, we don't know, but that, of course, that could justify that the Court go into the alternative avenues as set forth by the Appeals Chamber including a videolink. But we believe that this stage is not yet arrived. And it's the first delay in terms of the possibility of the Court to have now the time-frame for the restart of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In practical terms, it's the third delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: We agree, it's the third delay, but seen from the perspective of the prospect of the recovery, we have now the first concrete indication from an expert as to the time-frame the experts apparently need for the recovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I would like to ask the Defence if in the assessment, the various psychiatric and psychological assessments, the Defence recalls the reason by which no time, fixed time limits were given by the psychologist and the psychiatrist as to the recovery of Mr. Stanisic? Do you recall why the experts were reluctant to give exact time-frames for the prognosis of problems suffered by Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Knoops, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: -- I can briefly address that question on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Stanisic. Actually, the question as to the length of the recovery, a specialist would need to have a full recovery was never explored in depth as such. Secondly, it may be difficult for a expert to answer that question in view of the vicious circle of the illnesses Mr. Stanisic is suffering from and the interrelationship. Therefore I think the only person who can really answer Your Honours about how realistic is this time-frame is Dr. de Man. Therefore I said in my submissions he must have had experience with such a situation or is knowledgeable to come with this time-frame but it's, in our submission, the first expert who is concretely speaking about a time-frame for a recovery. And it strikes me that he specifically refers to at least three until six months, while the other experts indeed did not go into that discussion and were reluctant in terms of professional reluctance, reservations may be the better word, to give the Chamber a prognosis. Even what I recall Dr. Smit, the Court expert, was very reserved as to the time-frame. I believe she told the Court it could be a matter of weeks or months. That was the only guideline I believe that we got from her testimony. But again, this is the best evidence the Chamber has now in front of it, and therefore, we have to guess why the other experts were not capable of coming with a specific time-frame. And I agree, Your Honour, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I would like to refer the Defence to the reading of our decision when we evaluated the various experts diagnosis, and that's why the -- in the decision, we always refer to the need for a reassessment, dynamic reassessment of the situation of Mr. Stanisic in the absence of any clear-cut time limitation as to the prognosis of his illnesses. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour, if I may briefly address this last point. Of course my learned friend, Mr. Jordash, did not seek for revisitation of the application on the fitness as such. I think Your Honour rightfully observed that this time-frame which is now rather concrete as suggested by Dr. de Man and was not previously within the knowledge of the Chamber may, in addition to his additional diagnosis, be a new piece of forensic evidence which was not there on the 10th of March and may therefore justify the assessment Your Honours had in mind as a weekly assessment. It's merely a suggestion by me. We are not therefore revisiting -- asking the Court to revisit that decision of course, but we simply observe that this is also, in addition to the psychosis, the psychosis features, a new piece of forensic evidence in terms of the diagnosis and prognosis for a recovery of the depression. And this may justify the second option as we, as the Defence team, have referred to the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I would like also to just make a brief comment that no one of the experts were given, in their assessments to the Chamber, a time-frame even when asked specifically by our President on the various alternatives in relation to the legal dimensions of his illnesses as to enumeration, there were five or six options given by our President, yet I have to mention that in reading the assessment of Dr. de Man, it surprised me suddenly the time dimensions of his diagnosis. I'm saying "surprised" because in psychiatric literature, it's very uncommon just out of the -- in the course of an examination that lasted only a few minutes, to come with a prediction in exact terms of the duration of an illness which is not one illness but a complication as is recognised, of many dimensions, a multi-dimensional situation. I am saying this because really, the diagnosis, in many respects, while confirming the fact that there are not psychiatric dimensions, psychotic dimensions, structurally psychotic dimensions in the personality refers to occasional hallucinations of which -- of whose nature he has not elaborated because they were in consultations the impossibility to assess, if they were just night happenings or psychiatric hallucinations. And of course this brings the Chamber with alternatives so the Chamber might decide, you know, on his testimony. Thank you very much, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We might very well have to hear from Dr. de Man. This suggestion was made by the Prosecutor, to have a limited hearing. The Chamber will consider that, as we consider the various options that are open. A concern that I would have is that that hearing be limited to Dr. de Man, but I don't know whether the Prosecutor would be in a position to say now whether he would be satisfied with a hearing confined to Dr. de Man.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, forgive me if I was misunderstood. I was presenting a range of options starting with evaluation of a report and a decision based on a report. If that was insufficient, a limited hearing with respect to Dr. de Man. If that was insufficient, then may be something broader. So I'm not proposing at this stage that we automatically open it up a broader hearing and depending on what happened at that hearing, might make submissions that it is sufficient or may need to be broader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I thank the parties for their submissions which the Chamber has found quite helpful and we'll give a decision shortly. We are adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.23 p.m.
